guides.title: Core Build Starter Guide
guides.subtitle: From written requirements to a running application, in ten stages
guides.html:
The core build is the sequence an experienced developer follows to take an application from written requirements to a deployed system that keeps running. This guide teaches that sequence in ten stages, the reasoning behind each decision, and one worked example carried through every stage.

Audience

Developers building and running a full application, from those doing it for the first time to experienced developers who want the reasoning, the comparisons and the checklists. Two reading paths are given below

Prerequisites

Python and basic SQL. Git and the command line help; Working in Git covers what a team needs. Installed: Python, Node.js, PostgreSQL, Docker (for the integration tests), Git, and an editor with a debugger

Reading time

About 4 hours for the full guide, and about 2 hours on the experienced path. Allow one working session per stage when building alongside the guide

Version

3.1, learner edition, October 16, 2026

Companion

Core Build Facilitator Notes: session plans, the validation record and the review history

How to use this guide

Read the stages in order. Each stage uses the output of the one before it, and the guide teaches that order as much as the content of each stage.

What you will be able to do

After working through the guide and its example, you can:

  1. Write requirements that give each later stage what it needs, including the two load numbers and the operating requirements: audit, retention, recovery and acceptable downtime.
  2. Choose a stack one layer at a time, including the API style, and record the reason for each choice.
  3. Set version rules for the tools you depend on and for the API you publish.
  4. Lay out a backend and its repository, write its skeleton, use an AI assistant to fill function bodies, and review them for correctness and security.
  5. Connect a front end, design the database in detail from the fields the application uses, and decide from measurements which load layers to add.
  6. Plan the tests for each layer, choose a deployment strategy, and deploy the application as separate services through a sandbox.
  7. Operate the application after launch: logs, errors, rollbacks, backups, patches and secret rotation.
  8. Work on the same code as other developers through branches and pull requests, and resolve merge conflicts.

How each stage is laid out

Every stage has the same parts, in this order:

  • Decision in brief. A box with the decision, the input it uses, the default choice, the reason for it, when to choose differently, the output it produces, and how much of the stage a first application needs.
  • Steps. The questions to work through, in the order an experienced developer asks them.
  • Common mistakes. What goes wrong at this stage, including rules that are often misremembered.
  • Example. What the stage produces for the example application.
  • Checkpoint. What must be true before the next stage starts. Commit your work at each checkpoint.
  • Self-check. Questions with answers near the end of the guide.

Some stages add three kinds of block after the Steps:

  • Basics. Plain definitions of the terms the stage uses. On the full path, read them before the Steps; skip them if the terms are familiar.
  • Going deeper. A comparison of the options for one decision, with the strengths, the limits and when to use each one, and the default to use when no requirement points elsewhere.
  • Scenario. A situation and what to do about it. Choices are shown as rows in a table; procedures, such as resolving a merge conflict or rolling back a release, are shown as numbered steps with the commands.

Stages 8 and 9 also have a table headed Original practice and this guide. It records where this guide recommends something different from the practice it is based on, and why.

A first application

The First app row in each Decision in brief box says how much of the stage a first application needs. Stages 1, 2 and 4 to 7 are done in full. Stage 3 can be kept short. Stage 8 is usually a load test, a stress test and one decision table. Stages 9 and 10 are done in full, on the smallest deployment that meets the requirements. In the Going deeper sections, read the comparison for each decision your application faces; where no requirement points elsewhere, the default is enough.

What this guide does not cover

A specific cloud provider, container orchestration such as Kubernetes, and the internal configuration of the queue, cache and replication layers. Code appears only in the examples, as short illustrations of what a stage produces. Terms are defined in the Glossary near the end, and sources are cited by number, for example (Source 4).

At a glance

Figure 1. The ten stages and the output each one passes on

Stages 1 to 3 decide what to build and with what. Stages 4 to 7 build it and end with an application that runs on one machine. Stages 8 and 9 prepare it for real users and put it on servers. Stage 10 keeps it running after launch. Each box in Figure 1 names the output that the next stage uses. Working in Git, the chapter near the end of the guide, applies from Stage 4 on.

Why this order

Five rules set the order of the stages. Each one prevents a specific kind of rework.

  1. Requirements before tools. The stack is chosen to meet the requirements. A tool chosen first limits what the application can do, and the requirements then get changed to fit the tool.
  2. Structure before code. Versions, folders and interfaces are settled before any function body is written. Every file then has a known place and every function a known contract, which is what makes generated code reviewable.
  3. Skeleton, then screens, then tables. The backend skeleton runs first, against a stub data layer. The screens come next and settle what the front end sends. The tables are designed last, from the fields the screens and functions actually use. The usual alternative, designing the database first, produces tables for needs that were guessed.
  4. Measure before adding load layers. Every layer in Stage 8 is another service to deploy, monitor and maintain. Each one is added when a load test shows it is needed. Stage 8 comes before Stage 9 because the layers it adds (a queue, workers, and a Redis instance for the broker) change what Stage 9 deploys.
  5. Plan operations before launch, run them after. The operating requirements (audit, retention, recovery, downtime) are gathered in Stage 1, the audit table is built in Stage 7, and backups and logs are set up in Stage 9. Stage 10 comes last because it runs these routines on the live application, and each one is set up before the first incident that needs it.

Who decides what

The developer makes the decisions that require understanding the whole application. An AI assistant does work that can be checked against those decisions.

The example application

Every stage ends with an example that shows what the stage produces for one application, User Notices. The example uses situations that come up in most business applications: a list of records with a detail page, a sign-in that fails, a bulk send of 5,000 messages, a feature requested after launch, and a year of operation after launch.

User Notices is an internal application. Staff sign in, browse a list of registered users, open and edit a user's details, and schedule SMS notices to groups of users. One notice can go to up to 5,000 users at once. The messages go out through an external SMS provider's API. After launch, the team asks for an internal chatbot that answers staff questions about users and notices.

Figure 2. User Notices at the end of Stage 7

Figure 2 shows User Notices at the end of Stage 7, before any load work: the browser, the Next.js front end, the FastAPI backend, the PostgreSQL database, and the SMS provider outside the application. Stages 8 to 10 add to this picture.

DECIDE · STAGE 1 OF 10

Stage 1. Gather the requirements

DECISION IN BRIEF

Decision

What must the application do, for whom, and under what constraints?

Input

A request for an application, and access to the people who will use it

Default

Write the requirements down and settle them before thinking about any tool

Reason

Every later stage takes its input from this one. The stack is chosen against the requirements, not the other way around

Choose differently when

A throwaway prototype with no maintenance ahead can skip written requirements

Output

Screens, stored data, external services, two load numbers, constraints, the deployment target and the operating requirements, written down

First app

Do in full

Steps

  1. Screens. What does a user do in the application, screen by screen? List each screen and what happens on it. Stage 6 turns each screen into a page and a route.
  2. Data. What has to be stored and retrieved, including anything that must be logged? Which actions need an audit record of who did what, to which record and when? Stage 7 turns this list into fields and tables, including the audit table.
  3. External services. What does the application talk to outside itself: other services, APIs, message providers? Stage 2 chooses the API approach from this list.
  4. Load. How much load to expect, as two separate numbers: registered users, and requests at the same moment (concurrent requests). 100,000 registered users may produce 50 concurrent requests. Note how the load arrives: steady, or in bursts such as a scheduled bulk send. Stage 8 uses these numbers.
  5. Constraints and deployment target. Which tools are mandated, which database licenses are already held, where data is allowed to live, and where the application will run: a cloud provider or the organization's own servers. Stage 2 treats constraints as overriding its defaults, and Stages 8 and 9 build for the deployment target.
  6. Operating requirements. How long must each kind of record and log be kept? How much recent data may be lost if the database server fails (the recovery point), and how long may the application be down while it is restored (the recovery time)? When are users working, and how long may an update interrupt them? Stage 9 chooses the deployment strategy and the backups from these answers, and Stage 10 sets the retention, the restore tests and the update windows.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a framework or database before the requirements exist.
  • Recording load as one number. Registered users and concurrent requests lead to different decisions in Stage 8.
  • Leaving out bursts. A scheduled bulk send is a load pattern even when daily traffic is small.
  • Leaving out what must be logged. Logs are stored data and need tables in Stage 7.
  • Leaving out the operating requirements. Without a retention period, a recovery point and an acceptable downtime, Stages 9 and 10 have nothing to design the backups, the deployment strategy and the log settings against.

Self-check

  1. An application will have 80,000 registered users. What second number do you need before Stage 8, and why?
  2. A nightly job will send 10,000 reminder messages. Where does that belong in the requirements?
  3. Staff ask who changed a user's opt-in last week, and the application cannot say. Which requirement was missing, and which stages build what it needs?

DECIDE · STAGE 2 OF 10

Stage 2. Pick the stack

DECISION IN BRIEF

Decision

Which tool will each layer of the application use?

Input

The Stage 1 requirements and constraints

Default

Next.js for the front end, Python for the backend, PostgreSQL for the database, and FastAPI serving a REST API

Reason

Each layer is decided against one question from the requirements, and each answer limits the choices for the next: a Python backend means a Python API framework

Choose differently when

A Stage 1 constraint mandates another tool, a license is already held, or no cloud provider is allowed

Output

One tool per layer and the API style, each with its reason written next to it, and a list of the settings the application will read

First app

Do in full

Steps

  1. Front end. Is a front end needed at all? If so, is one HTML page enough? When the application has several pages with links between them (a users list that opens a user detail page), the default is Next.js with the App Router, where folders under app/ define the routes (Source 1).
  2. Backend language. What kind of work does the backend do? For AI work and calls to LLM APIs the default is Python, because most of the relevant libraries are Python libraries. Node.js supports the same LLM APIs and is a workable choice. Where the organization's finance or line-of-business systems are built on .NET, use .NET.
  3. Database. Is the data relational rows and columns, files, or both? The relational default is PostgreSQL unless the organization mandates another database; MSSQL, for example, needs licenses and organizational support. Files go to object storage: S3 when a cloud provider is allowed, otherwise a self-hosted S3-compatible store.
  4. API style. How do the front end and other programs talk to the backend, and does the server ever need to send something without being asked? The default is a REST API over HTTPS with JSON. Add another style only for the part of the application whose requirement needs it: updates pushed from the server, events sent by another system, or callers that need very different shapes of the same data (see Going deeper: Choosing an API style).
  5. API framework. For a Python backend the default is FastAPI, which describes the API in an OpenAPI document and shows it at /docs. Write each endpoint function as async def and use libraries that support await for network and database calls, so the server keeps handling other requests while one call waits. When a library has no await support, declare that endpoint with plain def. FastAPI then runs it in a threadpool so it does not block the server (Source 4).
  6. Settings. List the settings the application will read from its environment: the database connection string, the addresses of other services, API keys, the secret that signs session cookies, and the front end's address. Stage 4 creates the .env file that holds them.

BASICS API styles

An API style is the set of rules for how a client asks for something and how the answer comes back: what a request looks like, where it is sent, what format the answer uses, and whether the server can send data without a request.

  • Request and response. The client sends a request and waits for one answer. REST, GraphQL, gRPC and SOAP work this way.
  • Push. The server sends data when it has something new, over a connection the client keeps open. Server-Sent Events and WebSockets work this way.
  • Callback. Another system calls a URL in your application when an event happens on its side. Webhooks work this way.
  • Contract. A machine-readable description of the API that tools use to generate documentation, clients and tests: OpenAPI for REST, a schema for GraphQL, .proto files for gRPC, and WSDL for SOAP.

GOING DEEPER

Choosing an API style

Style

How it works

Strengths

Limits

Use when

REST over HTTPS with JSON

Each resource has a URL, and HTTP methods (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE) act on it. OpenAPI describes it (Source 29)

Every language, browser and tool can call it; GET responses can be cached; can be tested with curl or from /docs; versions sit in the path

A screen may need several calls, or receive fields it does not use; the server cannot send without a request

The default for screens that list, view and change records, and for APIs other teams call

Polling

The page repeats a REST GET request every few seconds

Plain REST; nothing new to run on the server

Updates arrive up to one interval late, and requests continue when nothing has changed

Progress that may be a few seconds late, watched by a few people at once

GraphQL

One endpoint, usually /graphql. The client sends a query naming the fields it wants, checked against a typed schema (Source 30)

One request returns exactly the fields a screen needs, across related types; the schema documents itself

HTTP caching needs GET requests, and long queries need persisted queries to fit in a URL; the server must limit query depth and cost; nested fields cause N+1 queries unless batched with a DataLoader (Sources 31 and 32)

Several kinds of client (web, mobile, partners) need different shapes of the same data, and REST endpoints keep being added for each screen

gRPC

Methods defined in .proto files; messages encoded as Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2; client and server code generated; streaming in either or both directions (Sources 33 and 34)

Compact binary messages; a strict contract; four call types, including two-way streaming

Browsers cannot call it directly and need gRPC-Web through a proxy, or Connect; binary messages are harder to inspect (Sources 35, 36 and 37)

Calls between internal services at high volume, or with streaming

WebSockets

The client opens one connection that stays open, and either side can send at any time (Source 38)

Low-latency messages in both directions

Each open connection is held by one server process, so with several processes a shared message layer such as Redis is needed to reach every client; the reverse proxy must pass the upgrade headers (Sources 39 and 40)

Chat, live collaboration, and anything where both sides send often

Server-Sent Events (SSE)

The server keeps an HTTP response open and writes events to it; the browser's EventSource reads them and reconnects on its own (Source 41)

Plain HTTP; automatic reconnection; FastAPI supports it directly from version 0.135.0 (Source 42)

Server to client only; text only; without HTTP/2, a browser allows 6 open connections per domain, shared by all its tabs (Source 43)

Live progress, status updates, notifications, and streaming a chatbot's answer

Webhooks

Another system sends an HTTP request to a URL in your application when an event happens, signed with a shared secret (Source 44)

No polling; the event arrives when it happens

The endpoint must check the signature, drop repeated deliveries by event id, answer quickly and do the work in a queue. Senders retry, so the same event can arrive more than once

Receiving events from a provider: delivery reports, payments, repository events

SOAP

XML messages described by a WSDL file (Sources 45 and 46)

Strict contracts and long-established tooling in older enterprise and government systems

Verbose; few new services offer it

Only to integrate with an existing system that offers nothing else. In Python, the zeep client reads the WSDL

Default. Start with REST. Add another style for one part of the application when a requirement calls for it, and keep REST for the rest. One application can serve REST to its screens, stream one page with SSE, and receive webhooks from a provider.

Questions to ask, in order:

  1. Is the caller a browser, a script or another team's system? Use REST.
  2. Must the server send updates without being asked? If only the server sends, use SSE. If both sides send often, use WebSockets.
  3. Does another system need to tell you when something happens on its side? Receive its webhooks, if that system can reach your application's network; otherwise ask its API on a schedule.
  4. Do several kinds of client need different shapes of the same data, and are REST endpoints multiplying for each screen? Consider GraphQL, with depth and cost limits.
  5. Are two internal services exchanging a high volume of calls, or streaming? Consider gRPC.
  6. Does an existing system you must call offer only SOAP? Use a SOAP client for that one integration.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a tool because it is new or familiar, without a reason tied to a requirement.
  • Using plain def to slow down calls to a server that rate limits them. Plain def functions also run concurrently, in a threadpool. Limit outbound calls with a client-side limiter, or with the task queue's rate limit setting in Stage 8.
  • Missing a Stage 1 constraint, such as a mandated database, and finding out at deployment.
  • Choosing GraphQL or gRPC for an application with one front end whose screens list and edit records. REST covers it with less code.
  • Asking the server for updates every second when Server-Sent Events can send them as they happen.
  • Accepting webhooks without checking the signature, or processing the same event twice.

DECIDE · STAGE 3 OF 10

Stage 3. Settle the versions

DECISION IN BRIEF

Decision

Which release of each tool will the project build on, and what counts as a breaking change to its own API?

Input

The Stage 2 stack

Default

For each platform component, a major version that has had time for fixes and has years of support left, on its latest minor release. The exact version of every dependency recorded. A new API version for any change that could break an existing client

Reason

An unsupported version becomes a continuity problem later, and dependencies without exact versions make two builds differ. Callers depend on the exact shape of what the API returns

Choose differently when

A small system that does not touch major areas of a tool can skip the detailed comparison between versions. Large or financial systems do it in full

Output

A version table with support end dates and the exact version of every dependency, a written breaking-change rule, and a patching rule. The versions go into lock files when the repository is created in Stage 4

First app

Keep short: the version table, the exact versions, a /v1 prefix and the written rule

Steps

  1. List the components. Everything from Stage 2 that has a version: the operating system, the language runtimes, the database, the frameworks and the main libraries. Components added later, such as Redis in Stage 8, join the table when they are added.
  2. Platform components. For components that publish support policies (PostgreSQL, Python, Node.js, Next.js), choose a major version that has had time for fixes and has years of support left. A major version released in the last few months has had less time for fixes and for other tools to be tested against it. Run the latest minor release of the chosen major version. PostgreSQL minor releases contain only fixes, and the project recommends always running the current minor release (Source 10).
  3. Compare with what is in use. If the organization already runs an older version, compare the two: what was added, what changed, what was removed. A version already out of support, such as PostgreSQL 12, needs a plan to move off it.
  4. Libraries. Libraries without support policies (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic and similar) get an exact version, are pinned in a lock file, and are updated deliberately, one at a time, with the tests run after each update. For Python, the lock file is a requirements.txt generated by pip-compile from requirements.in, so the libraries' own dependencies are pinned too.
  5. Compatibility. Confirm that the parts work together: the Python version, the packages in the project's virtual environment (Source 6), the database driver and the database version.
  6. Your own API. Write the rule for breaking changes. A breaking change is any change an existing client could fail on: a removed or renamed route or field, a changed type or meaning, a new required input, a changed error code, or a changed authentication requirement. An added optional field or a new route is not breaking. For a breaking change, release a new version, tell the clients before release, and keep the old version running while they move. The version usually sits in the path, /v1/users then /v2/users (Source 26).

BASICS Secrets

A secret is any value that gives access to something: a password, an API key, a token, a signing key, or a connection string that contains a password. The rules start with the first commit:

  • Secrets live in .env on each developer's machine and in the server's secrets file (Stage 9), never in the code or in any committed file.
  • .env.example lists every setting with a placeholder value, so the names are documented and the values are not.
  • A secret scanner such as gitleaks runs before each commit (Sources 48 and 49), and the repository host's push protection, where it is available, blocks pushes that contain a known kind of secret (Source 50).
  • A secret that reaches a commit is treated as exposed. Rotate it first (Stage 10), then remove it from the files in a new commit. Rewrite the history only when the organization requires it (Working in Git); rewriting does not remove copies already in other clones (Source 51).

BASICS Security terms

  • Authentication. Checking who the caller is, for example by the session cookie issued at sign-in.
  • Authorization. Checking what that caller may do, and to which record.
  • Injection. Input that ends up executed as part of a query or a command.
  • Dependency. A library the code installs. It is a supply chain risk when it is outdated, has been tampered with, or is not the package that was intended.
  • Cross-site scripting (XSS). Text that a user entered is shown on a page as code, and runs in other users' browsers.
  • Static analysis. A tool reads the code without running it and reports risky patterns.
  • OWASP. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, which publishes the risk lists and cheat sheets cited below.

Review every body for security as well as against its comment, whoever wrote it. Generated code needs the same review as a colleague's code; it is not a way around review, testing or static analysis (Source 60). Steps

  1. Fields. Walk through each screen and each function and write down every value it reads or writes, including what must be logged and audited. Finish the list before designing any table.
  2. Tables and columns. Group the fields into tables, one concept per table, each with a primary key. Give each column a type, decide whether it may be empty, set a default where one applies, and add the constraints that keep wrong values out (see Going deeper: Schema details). Under load, a table that holds too many concepts is one of the first things to split.
  3. Audit trail. Create the audit table from the Stage 1 audit requirement. The application may add and read audit rows but not change or delete them (see Going deeper: Audit trail).
  4. Views. A plain view is a saved query: it makes a join reusable and does not change its speed. A materialized view stores the result, which makes a slow dashboard query fast, but PostgreSQL updates it only when REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW runs, so the refresh has to be scheduled (Source 16). Add one when a measured query needs it.
  5. Indexes. Primary keys and unique constraints are indexed automatically. Foreign key columns are not, and usually should be (Sources 13 and 14). Index the columns in the most frequent WHERE and JOIN clauses. A multicolumn index helps when the query constrains its leading column, and PostgreSQL advises using them sparingly (Source 15). Every index adds work to each insert and update and takes storage, so remove indexes that no query uses (Source 12).
  6. Schema and migrations. Write the tables, views and indexes as SQLAlchemy models, have Alembic's autogenerate write a migration from them, review it, and apply it (the commands are in the Example). Every later change to the schema is a new migration. Give every migration a downgrade and run the round trip (upgrade, downgrade, upgrade) before committing. Each migration must work with the code before it and the code after it (see Going deeper: Changing a schema that is in use).
  7. Connect. The backend reaches PostgreSQL through a driver or ORM (for example SQLAlchemy over psycopg), using the connection string from .env. The migrations run as a database role that owns the tables, and the application logs in as a second role with only the privileges it needs. A database superuser creates the roles once in each environment, before the first migration (see the Example). The application reads DATABASE_URL, and migrations/env.py reads MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL, so the running application never holds the owner's password. Replace the Stage 5 stub, run the unit tests and the integration tests against PostgreSQL (Stage 9 lists them), and run the full request path from the browser.

BASICS Schema terms

  • Column type. The kind of value a column holds: text, a whole number, a point in time.
  • NULL. No value. NOT NULL means the column must always have one.
  • Default. The value used when an insert gives none.
  • Constraint. A rule the database checks on every insert and update: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY.
  • Role. A database account, unrelated to the staff roles (editor, viewer) in User Notices. The role that owns the tables and the role the application logs in as can be different.
  • Transaction. A group of statements that the database saves together, or not at all.
  • Trigger. A function the database runs on every insert, update or delete on a table.
  • Migration. One file that changes the schema. Its upgrade function makes the change, and its downgrade function reverses it.
  • Revision and head. The id Alembic gives each migration, and the newest revision. Each migration names the one before it in down_revision.
  • Round trip. Upgrade, downgrade, then upgrade again, to show that both directions work.
  • Rollback. Going back to the previous release of the code (Stage 9).

Changing a schema that is in use

During a deploy, and after a code rollback, one version of the code runs against the schema left by the other version's migrations. A migration is safe when the code before it and the code after it both work with the schema it leaves. Changes that would break the older code are split across releases: first expand (add the new structure and use it alongside the old), then contract (remove the old structure once nothing uses it). This is called expand and contract, or parallel change (Source 79).

Start each migration with op.execute("SET lock_timeout = '5s'"). A migration that waits longer than that for a lock then fails and can be run again, and the queries queued behind it are not held up.

Write a downgrade for every migration and run the round trip before committing. Alembic's autogenerate writes upgrade and downgrade functions, and its output always needs review (Source 82). A downgrade restores structure, not data: after a migration that drops a column, the downgrade can recreate the column but not its values. SCENARIO Renaming a column without breaking a rollback

The team wants users.phone renamed to phone_e164. Each release can be rolled back to the one before it.

  1. Release 1.5.0 (expand). A migration adds phone_e164, allowing NULL. The code writes both columns and still reads phone. A one-off job copies phone into phone_e164 for existing rows. Rolling back to 1.4.0 works: 1.4.0 ignores the new column.
  2. Release 1.6.0 (migrate). The code reads phone_e164 and still writes both. A migration makes phone_e164 NOT NULL. Rolling back to 1.5.0 works: 1.5.0 still writes both columns.
  3. Release 1.7.0 (stop writing). A migration removes NOT NULL from phone (ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN phone DROP NOT NULL), and the code removes phone from the SQLAlchemy model, so it neither reads nor writes it. Rolling back to 1.6.0 works: the column still exists, and 1.6.0 writes both columns.
  4. Release 1.8.0 (contract). After a backup, a migration drops phone. Rolling back to 1.7.0 works: 1.7.0's model has no phone column, so its queries do not name it.

Steps

  1. Load test and stress test. A load test sends the expected concurrency at the backend and confirms it holds. A stress test raises the concurrency until something fails, which gives the breaking point. Tools such as k6 or Locust run both. Run them on a machine sized like the deployment target, such as the server that will become the sandbox, not on a laptop. Until Stage 9 sets that server up, install PostgreSQL on it, copy the code and a .env with test values, and start the backend by hand with uvicorn for the test. Record the breaking point and the working level (the highest concurrency with no errors and acceptable response times), and plan for headroom above the expected load, for example twice the expected concurrency.
  2. Cheaper fixes. Before adding services, check the indexes, split tables that hold too many concepts, and review how the API routes are configured and how much load each one carries.
  3. Task queue. Work that is slow or arrives in bulk does not run inside a request. The application puts one job per unit of work into a broker, and separate worker processes take jobs from the queue. Celery uses Redis or RabbitMQ as its broker; ARQ uses Redis (Sources 21 and 23). Each worker's concurrency is a setting, and the rate of outbound calls is a separate setting (in Celery, a task's rate_limit, which applies per worker). Run the broker on its own Redis instance with no eviction policy, so queued jobs are never removed to make room for cache entries (Source 22). A job can be delivered more than once, so a task checks whether its work is already done before doing it.
  4. Rate limiting and cache. Rate limiting runs inside the application as middleware, with the counters in Redis so that every application process sees the same count (Source 24). Apply it to endpoints that receive many requests from one client. A Redis instance can also cache expensive reads. Redis runs as its own service, not inside the backend.
  5. Connection pooling. PostgreSQL accepts 100 connections by default, each costs memory, and the limit changes only at server start (Source 11). Drivers and ORMs already pool connections inside one process. Add PgBouncer, a connection pooler, when many processes each hold a pool and the total would exceed the limit. Its transaction mode shares connections most, but does not support session state such as SET commands, LISTEN, session-level advisory locks, SQL PREPARE or WITH HOLD cursors, and protocol-level prepared statements need its max_prepared_statements setting, so check what the driver and ORM need first (Source 20).
  6. Read replicas. Is the application read heavy or write heavy? PostgreSQL standby servers serve read-only queries, and all writes go to the primary (Source 18). The application, or a proxy, must send reads to the replicas. Replication is asynchronous by default, so a read sent right after a write may not see that write (Source 19).
  7. Sharding. Sharding splits the data across several database servers. It changes how every query is routed, so it comes after everything above has been evaluated. Partitioning is different: it splits a table on the same server and does not add capacity by itself (Source 17).
  8. Choose the product for each layer. For each layer the measurements call for, choose the product from the comparison in Going deeper: Choosing the load layers, check its license against the Stage 1 constraints, and add it to the Stage 3 version table with its support end date.

BASICS Load layers

  • Queue and broker. A queue holds jobs until a worker takes them. The broker is the service that keeps the queue, such as Redis or RabbitMQ.
  • Worker. A process that takes jobs from the queue and runs them.
  • Cache. A fast store of answers that can be rebuilt, so repeated reads skip the slow work.
  • Connection pooler. A service that shares a few database connections among many processes.
  • Read replica. A copy of the database that serves reads.
  • Partitioning and sharding. Splitting one table into parts on the same server, or splitting the data across several servers.
  • Load balancer. A service that spreads requests across several copies of a service.

Steps

  1. Test plan. For each layer of the application, decide which kinds of test cover it, using the table in Going deeper: Which test for which layer. The unit tests from Stages 5 to 7 are the first row.
  2. Unit, API and integration tests. Written in Stages 5 to 7 and extended here. They run on every push: the backend against stubs and against a real PostgreSQL, and the front end components on their own. Testcontainers starts PostgreSQL in Docker, so Docker is needed on developers' machines and on the CI runner.
  3. Functional testing. Name the people who will test and assign every scenario, including the edge cases, to one of them. A scenario is covered only when someone was assigned to it and has tested it.
  4. Regression script. After each merge to main, CI runs the full suite, including the end-to-end tests against the sandbox, and reports what broke.
  5. Security and accessibility. Run automated checks on every push: dependency checks (pip-audit, npm audit), static analysis of the code (Bandit, Semgrep) and secret scanning. Run the full security and accessibility audit before release and fix what it finds, for example an API endpoint that should not be reachable.
  6. Release build. CI (the repository's automated build) builds each merge to main into a release: the front end build, and the backend code with its pinned dependencies, as a package or a container image. The server receives a tested build, not a branch. When a build has passed the sandbox checks and is to go live, its commit is tagged with the release version (Working in Git).
  7. Server and secrets. Prepare each server with an account for each service that needs different access, the folders, and the firewall (see Going deeper: Preparing the server). The code belongs to root, with the service's account as its group, so a service can read and run its code but not change it. The secrets go in files outside the code folder that only root can read; systemd reads the application's file before starting each backend service. Every internal service listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Releases reach the server without a personal credential: the CI pipeline copies them with its own key to an account that can do nothing else (see the Example).
  8. Services. Run each part as its own service: the front end (a Node.js process), the backend (uvicorn with several worker processes), the task workers and scheduler, Redis and PostgreSQL. A process manager such as systemd starts each service at boot and restarts it if it stops; in systemd that takes Restart=on-failure in each unit file and systemctl enable for each unit. A reverse proxy such as nginx receives all traffic, handles TLS (HTTPS) and passes each request to the front end or the backend.
  9. Deployment strategy. Choose how a new release replaces the old one, from the Stage 1 update requirement: whether users can accept a short interruption, how many copies of each service run, and how quickly a bad release must be undone (see Going deeper: Choosing a deployment strategy). Keep the previous release on the server, so going back is a switch and not a rebuild, and test going back in the sandbox.
  10. Before the first user. Run the migrations once in each deploy, as the role that owns the tables, before the backend services start, not in the application's startup code, where several processes would run them at the same time. Add a health check endpoint. The services write their logs to standard output, and journald, the log store that comes with systemd, keeps them. Schedule database backups, copy each one off the server (see Going deeper: Backups off the server), and restore one as a test.
  11. Sandbox. Keep a sandbox (a staging environment) built from the same repository, with its own database, its own secrets and its own deployment. Every change goes to the sandbox first, and the same build is then promoted to live. The sandbox cannot reach live data or send messages to real users (see Going deeper: Sandbox and live).

BASICS Server terms

  • root and sudo. root is the administrator account on a Linux server. sudo runs one command as root, or as another account with -u.
  • Owner, group and mode. Every file has an owner and a group. Its mode says what the owner, the group and everyone else may do with it: read, write, or run (execute). In a mode such as 640, 6 is read and write, 4 is read only, and 0 is no access (Source 107).
  • Symbolic link. A file that points to another file or folder. /opt/user-notices/current is one.
  • systemd unit. A file in /etc/systemd/system/ that tells systemd how to start one service. systemctl start, stop, restart and status act on it, and journalctl -u shows its output.
  • Port and 127.0.0.1. A service listens on a port number. A service bound to 127.0.0.1 can be reached only from the same server.
  • SSH key. A pair of files used to log in without a password. The private key stays with the person or the pipeline; the public key goes on the server.
  • TLS certificate and private key. The certificate shows browsers the server's name. The private key stays on the server and proves that the server holds the certificate.
  • Firewall. Rules on the server that decide which ports other machines can reach.

In each unit, ProtectSystem=strict makes most of the file system read-only for the service, apart from the paths in ReadWritePaths= and the folders systemd creates for it with StateDirectory= and CacheDirectory=.

BASICS Deployment terms

  • Release and deploy. A release is a tested build with a version number. Deploying puts a release on the servers. A feature flag can keep new behavior switched off after the deploy and switch it on later.
  • Promote. Deploy to live the same build that passed in the sandbox.
  • Downtime. Time when users cannot use the application.
  • Instance. One running copy of a service.
  • Rollback. Going back to the previous release after a bad one.
  • Both versions at once. In every strategy except big bang, the old and new versions run at the same time. After any rollback, the old code runs against the new schema. Either way, the database must work with both versions (Stage 7, expand and contract). The same holds for queued jobs: jobs queued by one release are run by the next release's workers, and after a rollback by the previous one's. Change a task's name or arguments the same way: add the new form first, and remove the old one a release later.

Rules for every method:

  • Copy each backup off the database server, to a machine the database server cannot delete from, for example a backup server that pulls the files.
  • Encrypt backups that leave the server, and keep the key apart from the backups.
  • Keep one copy offline or off-site (Sources 117 and 122).
  • Back up what the database does not hold: the roles, the server configuration, and the secrets. The secrets go to the organization's secret store, not with the data.
  • A backup counts only once a restore from it has worked. Restore one before go-live, then every month (Stage 10).
  • Time the backup and the pull against the recovery point: a failure between the dump and the pull loses that dump too.

Common mistakes

  • A personal access token (PAT) on the production server.
  • Running the backend from a shell session instead of under a process manager.
  • Testing everything through the browser, so the suite is slow and fails for reasons unrelated to the change.
  • Treating a coverage percentage as the goal.
  • Copying live personal data, or the live SMS key, into the sandbox.
  • A secrets file inside the code folder, or readable by every account on the server.
  • Code files that the service's own account can change.
  • Choosing a zero-downtime strategy without making the migrations and the queued jobs work with both versions.
  • Mirroring requests that send messages or change data to a shadow copy.
  • No database backups, backups kept only on the database server, or backups that were never restored as a test.
  • Changing the schema on the server by hand.
  • Deploying a branch instead of a tested release.

The release is one file built by CI: the backend code, requirements.txt, a wheels/ folder written by pip wheel -r requirements.txt -w wheels on the runner (which runs the same Ubuntu release and Python version as the servers), and the front end's standalone build with public/ and .next/static/ copied into it (Source 123). A virtual environment records its own absolute path and cannot be moved (Source 6), so the deploy script creates it on the server. The pipeline copies the release over SSH to a deploy account on the server. That account can write only to /opt/user-notices/incoming/ and can run only /usr/local/sbin/user-notices-deploy through sudo, by one line in /etc/sudoers.d/user-notices. An administrator installs that script from the reviewed repository; the pipeline does not copy it. Each Stage 1 screen has an assigned owner for its functional scenarios. The sandbox holds made-up users, the SMS provider's test key and the four testers' numbers in SMS_ALLOWLIST.

Deployment strategy: big bang outside working hours, with release folders. Each release is unpacked into /opt/user-notices/releases/ under its version, and /opt/user-notices/current links to the active one. The deploy script, deploy/deploy.sh, installed on the server as /usr/local/sbin/user-notices-deploy, runs as root and does the following, in order:

  1. Unpack the release from /opt/user-notices/incoming/ into /opt/user-notices/releases/1.5.0/, create the virtual environment in the release folder with python3.14 -m venv, install the wheels with the environment's pip install --no-index --find-links wheels -r requirements.txt, compile the bytecode cache with the environment's python -m compileall -q app (the service cannot write to the release folder, so the cache is written now), and then set the owners and modes from the permissions table.
  2. Stop the beat and worker services. Celery finishes the tasks in progress, and queued jobs stay in Redis.
  3. Back up the database: sudo -u postgres pg_dump --format=custom --file=/var/backups/user-notices/before-1.5.0.dump usernotices.
  4. Stop the front end and the API.
  5. Record the current revision with alembic current, then run alembic upgrade head from the new release's backend folder, as usernotices_owner, with the connection string from /etc/user-notices/migrate.env. Alembic runs the upgrade in a transaction, so if a migration fails, PostgreSQL rolls it back; the script then starts the previous release unchanged and stops.
  6. Switch the link: ln -sfn /opt/user-notices/releases/1.5.0 /opt/user-notices/current.
  7. Start the API, the front end, the workers and beat.
  8. Call GET /v1/health every 5 seconds for up to 60 seconds, then sign in with the account in /etc/user-notices/smoke.env and call GET /v1/users. If either fails, switch the link back and start the previous release.

deploy.sh --rollback runs steps 2, 4, 6 and 7 for the previous release, so the workers and beat also go back to the previous code. A switch back runs the previous code against the migrated schema, so every migration follows expand and contract. Users are interrupted from step 4 until step 7 completes, within the 5 minutes Stage 1 allows.

Backups: at 01:00 each night, a systemd timer runs pg_dump --format=custom and pg_dumpall --globals-only as the postgres account, into /var/backups/user-notices, and deletes local dumps older than 3 days. At 01:30 the organization's backup server pulls the files over SSH as the usernotices-backup account, whose key is limited in authorized_keys to reading that folder (command="rrsync -ro /var/backups/user-notices/"). The backup server encrypts the files and keeps them for 35 days; the first backup of each month also goes to offline storage at another site and is kept for a year. The newest copy off the server is at most 24 hours and 30 minutes old, which meets the Stage 1 recovery point because staff change data only between 8:00 and 18:00: a failure at any hour loses at most one working day of edits. A restore into a scratch database before go-live took 20 minutes.

DECISION IN BRIEF

Decision

How is the application kept running, recoverable and current after launch?

Input

The live application and the sandbox from Stage 9, the Stage 1 retention, recovery and update requirements, and the Stage 3 version table and patching rule

Default

Set a retention period for each kind of log; send errors to an error tracker and watch the servers with a monitoring tool, both alerting a named person; write the rollback procedure before it is needed; fix forward rather than downgrade when data is involved; restore a backup every month; patch on a calendar, through the sandbox; rotate secrets on a schedule and whenever one may have been exposed

Reason

Most of an application's life comes after launch. Each routine is cheaper to set up before the first incident that needs it than during that incident

Choose differently when

Managed services take over part of the work, such as a cloud provider's database backups or log storage. The routines stay; the tools change

Output

A runbook with the retention table, the alert rules, the rollback procedure, the restore record, the patch calendar and the rotation schedule, each with an owner, and each routine run once

First app

Do in full, at the smallest scale: journald retention, one error tracker, a scheduled check script for the other alerts, the rollback steps, nightly off-server backups with a monthly restore, a monthly update window and a yearly rotation

Steps

  1. Logs and retention. List each kind of log, where it is kept, who reads it and how long it is kept, from the Stage 1 retention requirement. Set the retention in the tool that keeps each one: journald for the services' output, logrotate for nginx's files, and a scheduled job for the audit and send records in the database. Logs are not deleted before the required period ends, and are not kept long after it (Sources 64 and 125). Read a service's output with journalctl -u user-notices-api --since "1 hour ago".
  2. Error tracking. Send every unhandled error from the backend and the front end to an error tracker, which groups repeated errors and shows the stack trace, the release and how many users were affected. Keep personal data out of the events (see Going deeper: Logs, errors and alerts).
  3. Monitoring and alerts. The error tracker alerts on errors only. Disk space, queue length, a backup that did not arrive and a certificate close to expiry need a monitoring tool: the organization's existing one, or Prometheus with Alertmanager. For a first application, a script run by a systemd timer every 5 minutes can check each value and send the email. The health check is called from another server, so a failure is reported even when the live server is down. The four signals to watch for any service are latency, traffic, errors and saturation (Source 126).
  4. Rollback procedure. Write the steps before they are needed, and run them once in the sandbox. Going back to the previous release is a switch when the release folders are kept (Stage 9). Write down who decides to roll back, and the check that confirms the rollback worked.
  5. Migrating backwards. For each release, record how its migrations would be undone: left in place, downgraded, fixed forward, or restored (see Going deeper: Undoing a migration). The deploy script backs up the database before migrating (Stage 9).
  6. Backups and restores. Check each morning that last night's backup ran and reached the backup server. Each month, restore the latest backup into a scratch database, check it, record how long the restore took against the Stage 1 recovery time, and drop the scratch database. A restore holds live personal data, so it runs on the live server or on a server with the same access rules, never in the sandbox. Delete backups that are older than the retention period.
  7. Patching. Put the Stage 3 patching rule on a calendar: operating system security updates, the database's minor releases, language runtime patches and library updates (see Going deeper: Patching calendar). Operating system security updates install themselves each day, apart from the packages the application depends on, which go through the sandbox first. A critical security fix is applied outside the calendar. Plan each major upgrade before the support end date in the Stage 3 version table.
  8. Secret rotation. Replace each secret on a schedule, and at once when it may have been exposed or when someone who could read it leaves. Where the application allows it, rotate with an overlap: create the new secret, deploy it, confirm it works, then revoke the old one (see Going deeper: Rotating secrets).
  9. Incidents. Record each incident in the incident log: what users saw, the timeline, the cause, the fix and the follow-up actions. Review it without assigning blame, so the discussion stays on the causes and their fixes (Source 127).

BASICS Operations terms

  • Fix forward. Correcting a problem with a new release instead of going back to the previous one.
  • Patch. A release that fixes bugs or security problems without adding features.
  • Rotation. Replacing a secret with a new one, then revoking the old one.

SCENARIO A release breaks the Users list

At 19:10, after the 19:00 deploy of release 1.4.0, the error tracker alerts: GET /v1/users returns 500 for every request. The release's only migration added a column.

  1. The developer on duty decides to roll back, as the runbook allows for an error on a main screen.
  2. Roll back: deploy.sh --rollback switches current to release 1.3.2 and restarts the services.
  3. Check: GET /v1/health returns 200, the Users list loads, and the error tracker shows no new errors from 1.3.2.
  4. Leave the migration in place. It only added a column, which 1.3.2 ignores.
  5. The next day, reproduce the failure in the sandbox, add the test that would have caught it, and release 1.4.1 through the sandbox.
  6. Record the incident and review it.

SCENARIO A migration that damaged data

Release 2.0.0 converted every notice text to a new format. A bug in the conversion cut 300 long texts short.

  1. Check what the downgrade does: it converts the format back, but cannot restore the characters that were cut.
  2. Restore the dump the deploy script took before the migration into a scratch database on the live server: createdb notices_scratch, then pg_restore --dbname=notices_scratch with the file before-2.0.0.dump.
  3. Copy the original texts of the 300 notices, by id, into a temporary table in the live database.
  4. Fix forward: a one-off script, reviewed like any other change and run in the sandbox first, writes the original texts back to those rows and adds an audit row for each. The texts stay out of the repository.
  5. Drop the scratch database, add a test for the conversion with a long text, and record the incident.

SCENARIO The live server's disk fails

PostgreSQL runs on the live server, so the database, the Redis queue, the secrets files, the TLS key and the release folders are lost together.

  1. Record the incident, and tell staff that the application is unavailable and when it is expected back, within the 8-hour recovery time.
  2. Prepare a replacement server as in Stage 9 (Going deeper: Preparing the server).
  3. Restore the secrets files and the TLS certificate and key from the organization's secret store.
  4. Copy the latest backup from the backup server and decrypt it. Restore the roles from the pg_dumpall output with sudo -u postgres psql -f and the file name (the error that the role postgres already exists can be ignored), then create the database and run pg_restore.
  5. Deploy the release that was live with the deploy script, then stop the beat and worker services before going on.
  6. List the notices due after the backup: SELECT id, send_at, status FROM notices WHERE send_at >= '2026-11-20 01:00+00' AND status IN ('scheduled', 'sending'); using the backup's date and time. Compare each one with the SMS provider's records, and set status to 'sent' for each one the provider already sent, so it does not go out twice.
  7. Start the workers and beat. Check the health endpoint, the Users list, and a test send to a group that holds only a tester's phone.
  8. Changes made after the 01:00 backup are lost. Tell staff which period to check and re-enter.
  9. Record how long the recovery took, against the recovery time. Rebuild the sandbox server from the runbook once a year, so the time for a full rebuild is known.

SCENARIO The secrets file appears in a screenshot

A developer posts a screenshot of /etc/user-notices/backend.env from the live server in a team chat.

  1. Delete the screenshot from the chat. Treat every secret in the file as exposed: the SMS key, the database password, the session signing secret and the Redis password. Rotate them now rather than in the next window.
  2. Create a new SMS key at the provider, put it in backend.env, restart the workers and the API, and send a test to a tester's phone.
  3. Revoke the old key at the provider.
  4. Rotate the database password with the two roles and end the old role's sessions, change the Redis password, and replace the session signing secret, which signs every staff member out.
  5. Check the provider's usage records for sends the application did not make.
  6. Record the incident.

SCENARIO A critical security fix for the front end framework

An advisory announces a critical vulnerability in Next.js 16, fixed in a new patch release.

  1. Read the advisory: which versions and which kinds of deployment are affected, whether there is a workaround, and whether the flaw is being exploited.
  2. On a branch, install the fixed version with npm install next@ followed by the version the advisory names. package.json and package-lock.json both change.
  3. Open a pull request; CI runs the tests and the audits.
  4. After the merge, the sandbox receives the release and the end-to-end journeys run.
  5. Promote the same build to live within two working days, outside working hours, or the same day if the flaw is being exploited.
  6. If the flaw let attackers run code on the server, rotate every secret the affected service's account could read, as the advisory for CVE-2025-66478 recommended.

SCENARIO A developer with server access leaves

  1. Remove their accounts and SSH keys: both servers, the backup server, the repository host, the CI system, the error tracker and the SMS provider's console.
  2. Rotate every secret they could read: the database passwords, including usernotices_owner's, the SMS key, the session secret and the Redis password. If they had root on the live server, also replace the TLS key and the backup account's SSH key.
  3. Check that no pipeline, scheduled job or key depends on their personal account.
  4. Record the changes.

Adding a module later

A new requirement after launch is not a new project. It runs through the same stages: its requirements first, then its screens.

In the main build, the backend skeleton came before the screens because the structure did not exist yet. For a module, the structure exists, so after its requirements the module's screens come first and define the backend calls it needs. The tables still come after the calls, for the same reason as in the main build.

  1. Pause load work. Finish or pause any load or stress testing in progress, so its measurements are not mixed with the change.
  2. Requirements, stack and versions (Stages 1 to 3). Write the module's screens, data, load and constraints. Check them against the existing stack and the Stage 1 constraints, and add any new tool to the version table.
  3. Inside or separate. A module that shares the application's data and is changed and deployed with it belongs inside the application. Build it as a separate system only when it is unrelated to the existing one.
  4. Screens (Stage 6). Design the module's screens, then its pages and routes.
  5. Backend (Stages 4 and 5). Decide which calls the screens make and which router and service folder own them, and add them to the main.py index. Then the skeleton, the assistant, the review and the unit tests, as before.
  6. Tables (Stage 7). Decide which tables the module reads, which it changes and which it adds, and apply the change as a migration.
  7. Load (Stage 8). Add rate limiting and caching for its endpoints, and queue any bulk work, where the load test calls for it.
  8. Test and deploy (Stage 9). Add the module's tests at each layer, run the regression script and the security and accessibility checks, and promote the release through the sandbox.

Working in Git

Git records every change to the code and lets several developers change the same files at the same time. This chapter covers what a team needs from Stage 4 on: the daily loop, the team rules, the ways to merge, how to undo a change, and what to do when two people's changes collide. The commands are for Git 2.56. Hosting features use GitHub's names; other hosts offer the same features under similar names.

DECISION IN BRIEF

Decision

How do several developers change the same code without losing work or breaking main?

Input

The repository and the branch rules from Stage 4

Default

GitHub flow: main always passes its tests. Every change is made on a short-lived branch and reaches main through a pull request that passes CI and has one approving review. Pull requests are squash-merged, and history that others have pulled is never rewritten

Reason

Small branches conflict less often, review catches what tests miss, and a main branch that always passes can be released at any time

Choose differently when

A product with several supported versions keeps a branch per version and moves fixes between them with cherry-pick. A team that merges many times a day behind feature flags commits to the main branch directly, which is called trunk-based development (Source 143)

Output

Branch protection on main, a pull request template, CODEOWNERS, tagged releases, and a team that can resolve a conflict and undo a change safely

First app

Do in full. With one developer, set the required approvals to 0, keep the pull requests and the required checks, and review each pull request yourself against the Stage 5 checklist

Steps

  1. Start from an up-to-date main. git switch main, then git pull.
  2. One branch per change. git switch -c notice-preview. Keep the branch to one change, and merge it within a day or two; branches that live for weeks accumulate conflicts.
  3. Commit in small steps. Stage the changes with git add -p, which shows each changed block and asks what to do with it (y stages it, n leaves it out, s splits it, q stops). git diff --staged shows what the commit will contain. Write a message that says what the change does.
  4. Commit files that belong together in the same commit. package.json with package-lock.json, requirements.in with requirements.txt, a migration with the model change it applies (Stage 7), and main.py with the router it lists.
  5. Push and open a pull request. git push -u origin notice-preview, then open the pull request on the hosting service's page for the branch, or with gh pr create (Source 144). CI runs the tests and the checks.
  6. Review. Another developer reviews the change against the Stage 5 security checklist. The author does not approve their own pull request.
  7. Bring the branch up to date before merging. If main has moved on, update the branch (Scenario: Your branch is behind main) and run the tests again.
  8. Merge and clean up. Squash and merge on the hosting service, and delete the branch there. Then git switch main, git pull, and git branch -D notice-preview; git branch -d refuses after a squash merge, because main holds a new commit rather than the branch's commits (Source 162).
  9. Tag each release. CI builds every merge to main and deploys it to the sandbox. When a build has passed the sandbox checks and is to go live, tag its commit: git tag -a v1.4.0 7d41e0b -m "Release 1.4.0", then git push origin v1.4.0. The live deploy installs that commit's build into a release folder named 1.4.0.

The daily loop, as commands:

git switch main

git pull # bring main up to date

git switch -c notice-preview # a branch for one change

git add -p # review and stage the changes

git commit -m "Show a preview of the notice before saving"

git push -u origin notice-preview # then open a pull request

BASICS Git terms

  • Repository. The project's files and their full history.
  • Commit. A saved set of changes, with a message and an id (a hash such as 3f2c9a1).
  • Branch. A movable name for a line of commits. main is the shared branch that releases are built from.
  • Remote. The copy of the repository on the hosting service, usually called origin. git push sends commits to it; git fetch and git pull bring commits from it.
  • Pull request. A request to merge a branch into main, where other developers review the change and CI runs the tests.
  • Merge. Combining the changes from two branches. When both changed the same lines, Git cannot choose between them and reports a merge conflict.
  • Tag. A fixed name for one commit, used to mark releases such as v1.4.0.
  • Staging area. The changes chosen for the next commit. git add puts changes there.
  • HEAD. The commit your working copy is on, usually the tip of the current branch.
  • origin/main. Your copy of the remote's main, as of your last git fetch.
  • Force push. A push that replaces the remote branch's commits with yours, used only after a rebase of your own branch.
  • Hotfix. A fix made for the release that is live, while main holds newer work.

SCENARIO Two people change the same file, on different lines

Developer A changes schedule_notice in services/notices.py. Developer B changes list_notices in the same file and merges first.

  1. Developer A updates the branch: git fetch, then git rebase origin/main. Git combines the two changes without a conflict, because they touch different lines.
  2. Run the tests. A merge without a conflict can still break the code, for example when B renamed a function that A's new code calls.
  3. Push with git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes, and continue the review.

SCENARIO Two people change the same lines

Developer A changed the error message for a past send time. Developer B changed the same check to allow a 5-minute grace period, and merged first. A brings main into the branch:

git fetch

git merge origin/main

CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in backend/app/services/notices.py

Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

The file now holds both versions between conflict markers:

<<<<<<< HEAD

if send_at < now:

raise ValueError("The send time must be in the future")

=======

if send_at < now - timedelta(minutes=5):

raise ValueError("Send time is in the past")

>>>>>>> origin/main

  1. Read both sides. In a merge, the part above the ======= line is your branch (HEAD), and the part below is main's version (Source 145). In a rebase the two are swapped: the part above is main with your earlier commits already replayed, and the part below is your commit being replayed. The labels after <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> name each side. To stop and put the branch back as it was, run git merge --abort, or git rebase --abort during a rebase.
  2. Decide what the code should do. Here it should do both: keep B's grace period and A's message.
  3. Edit the lines to the final version and delete the three marker lines:

if send_at < now - timedelta(minutes=5):

raise ValueError("The send time must be in the future")

  1. Run the tests, including the unit test for past send times, and update the test if the grace period changes what it expects.
  2. Mark the file resolved with git add backend/app/services/notices.py, finish with git commit, and push.

Two settings help with conflicts. git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 also shows the original lines, so it is clear what each side changed. git config --global rerere.enabled true makes Git remember how you resolved a conflict and reuse the resolution if the same conflict appears again (Sources 150 and 151).

SCENARIO Your branch is behind main

Only you have worked on the branch, and main has moved on since you started.

git fetch

git rebase origin/main

# for each conflict: fix the file, git add it, then

git rebase --continue

git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes

During the rebase, the part of a conflict above the ======= line is main and the part below is your commit; git rebase --abort puts the branch back as it was. If someone else has pulled your branch, use git merge origin/main instead, and push without force.

SCENARIO Two branches each add a migration

Both branches added an Alembic migration whose parent was the same revision. After both merge, the migration history has two heads, and alembic upgrade head stops with an error.

  1. Prevent it: CI runs pytest-alembic's single-head test (Stage 9), and the branch rules require a branch to be up to date with main before it merges. The second pull request then runs its checks with the first migration in place, and fails before it merges.
  2. Fix it on the second branch: find the first branch's revision with alembic heads or alembic history, set the second migration's down_revision to it, so the history is one line again, and run the round trip.
  3. Or, if both are already merged, create a merge migration with alembic merge -m "merge heads" heads. It has both revisions as parents (Source 152). Check that the two migrations do not change the same table in conflicting ways.

SCENARIO A conflict in package-lock.json

Both branches added a front end package, and the lock file has a conflict.

  1. Resolve package.json by hand, keeping both packages.
  2. Run npm install. npm resolves the conflicts in package-lock.json and writes a lock file that includes both branches' packages. npm's documentation describes this for npm 5.7.0 and later (Source 153).
  3. Commit both files. In CI, npm ci stops with an error if they disagree.

For the backend, resolve requirements.in by hand, take main's lock file with git checkout origin/main -- backend/requirements.txt, then run pip-compile from the backend folder. It keeps main's pinned versions and adds the packages from both branches. Do not edit either lock file by hand.

SCENARIO A fix for live while main is not ready

Release 1.4.0 is live. main already holds unfinished work for 1.5, and a bug in 1.4.0 must be fixed today.

  1. Create a release branch from the tag, if it does not exist yet, and push it: git switch -c release-1.4 v1.4.0, then git push -u origin release-1.4. Give it the same branch rules as main.
  2. Branch from it with git switch -c hotfix-1.4.1. Fix the bug, add a test and commit. Note the commit id, for example 5e8d2f7.
  3. Push and open a pull request into release-1.4; it is reviewed like any other change. After the merge, CI builds release 1.4.1 from release-1.4 and deploys it to the sandbox. Once the checks pass, the same build is promoted to live and its commit is tagged v1.4.1.
  4. Bring the fix to main: from an up-to-date main, git switch -c port-hotfix-1.4.1, then git cherry-pick -x 5e8d2f7, push, and open a pull request. The -x option adds a line with the original commit's full id, "(cherry picked from commit 5e8d2f7...)", to the message, so the two commits can be matched later (Source 154). If the fix includes a migration, set its down_revision to main's head in the port, as in Scenario: Two branches each add a migration.

Documentation and working rhythm

These practices run alongside the stages.

What to document

  • API calls. Every call the front end makes, with its route and version.
  • Database schema. The tables and what each holds, kept current by the migrations.
  • Front end routing. The routes and the reasons for them.
  • Distributed components. The queue, cache, pooler and replicas, and how each is deployed.
  • Operations runbook. The Stage 10 routines: retention, alerts, rollback, restores, patching and rotation, each with its owner.

Keep this at a high level. Developers work out the detail from the code, and documentation that covers every line goes out of date. The main.py index is the entry point to the detail.

AI change log

When you ask an assistant to write or change a function, ask it in the same prompt to add an entry to one log file: what it decided, what broke, why, and how it was fixed. Keep the file for the life of the project. It can be read directly, or given back to an assistant to produce documentation. Plan for its size: an assistant that reads the whole log at the start of a session spends part of its context on it, and in one long-running project the log took about a quarter of the available context.

Time and sessions

Typical times, from the practice this guide is based on:

  • Prototype. A throwaway application with no maintenance ahead can be generated in 5 to 10 minutes.
  • Maintained application. Write the architecture by hand first, so that every decision is understood. Then give the written design to an assistant with an instruction to find its weaknesses, and revise. For a small application, plan about two days for the architecture and the boilerplate.
  • Session length. Work in uninterrupted sessions of four to five hours. A session broken in the middle of a structure has to restart from the point where the design was last understood.

  2. git fetch, then git rebase origin/main, resolving any conflicts (during a rebase, the part above ======= is main). Then git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes, which refuses if the remote branch holds commits your branch does not include.
  3. Revert it: create a branch from main, run git revert with the squash commit's id, and merge the revert through a pull request. Do not reset main and force push.

Layer that tracks work and redelivers Optional layer

How to read it

Each column is one stack. A job moves down from the producer to the worker, and the word beside each up arrow is what the lower layer sends back. The shaded box is the layer that tracks jobs in progress and redelivers a job when a worker dies. In the arq column that logic is in the arq library, and Redis only stores the state. In the RabbitMQ and SQS columns the holder does it, and the worker reports back with an ack (RabbitMQ) or a delete call (SQS). All three can deliver a job more than once, so task code should be safe to run twice.

When to pick each

arq on Redis: Pick it when you have a Python asyncio app that already runs Redis, job volume is modest, and you do not want to add another service. After a hard worker crash, a job runs again only after its in-progress marker expires (the longest job timeout plus 10 seconds, 310 seconds by default). arq is in maintenance only mode: the maintainers fix critical security issues and say not to expect other new work.

RabbitMQ: Pick it when you need routing (exchanges, topics, fan-out), priorities, or workers in several languages, and you can operate a broker. RabbitMQ requeues unacked jobs when the worker's channel or connection closes.

SQS: Pick it when you are on AWS and do not want to run a broker. SQS redelivers only when the visibility timeout expires (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours), so set the timeout longer than your longest job.

Sources, checked October 11, 2026

  • arq maintenance status: github.com/python-arq/arq/issues/510
  • arq documentation and source, version 0.28.0: arq-docs.helpmanual.io
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • SQS visibility timeout: docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html

Where the outbox fits

Piece added by the outbox pattern

How to read it

Without the outbox, the app writes the order to PostgreSQL and the job to the holder as two separate writes, and a failure between them can leave an order with no job. With the outbox, the app does not write the job to the holder. It writes the order and an outbox row to its own PostgreSQL database in one transaction, so both are saved or neither is. The relay is a separate small process, like a worker but on the sending side. It polls the outbox table, forwards each job to the holder, and marks the row as sent.

How it fits the three stacks

Holder: The relay forwards each job to the one holder the stack uses. It enqueues with arq, publishes to RabbitMQ, or calls SendMessage on SQS, which is the step the producer does in panel 1. From the holder down, each stack is the same as in panel 1.

Scope: The outbox covers the step where a job is created. The three stacks differ in who tracks delivery after the job is in the holder. These are separate steps, so the outbox is the same for all three.

Database: The outbox table is in the app's own PostgreSQL database, the same database as the orders table. It is not in Redis, and an outbox row is not a job in the queue until the relay forwards it.

Duplicates: The relay can forward a job more than once, for example if it stops after forwarding a job and before marking the row as sent. Task code should be safe to run twice, as in panel 1.

Sources, checked October 11, 2026
